rv.q: From there it just gets more delightfully weird and endlessly inventive.
Inventive, mischievous and thrilling — this is children’s theatre that could take on Pixar.

Georgia Lowe’s design is full of exhilaratingly subversive touches like this, finding a perfect balance between lo-fi silliness and technically impressive effects that turn the Dorfman’s small stage into a place of wonder.
It's not a total smash. Twenty minutes could be lopped off, the dance numbers are a bit loose and some singing has a strong whiff of 'have a go'.
Amy Hodge's production – well-meaning, colourful and jolly as it is – is also half-baked.
Time and again, quirky detail is prioritised over clarity of storytelling.
All seem to be relishing the writing as much as a young reader who has just discovered, with a delighted shriek of laughter, that you can put pretty much anything you like in a book.
The result is a scattershot, uproarious, neon-bright delight that will transport children while also making the adults laugh rather more than they might have been expecting.
There's no doubt this show is a lot of fun.

Andy Stanton's laugh out loud children's books about a disgusting villain called Mr Gum and the surreal town of Lamonic Bibber have always been more about the wacky world and wordsmithery than the plot. So how would their cultish humour translate into a stage musical?

cn.t: Critics are divided on this aggressively quirky musical adaptation: some praise its inventive weirdness and meta-theatrical humor, while others find its eccentric flourishes prioritize style over clear storytelling.
